```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r attach}
library(priogridR)
```

Spatial analyses often require choices about which cells count as neighbors,
how strongly neighbors are weighted, and whether observations from different
periods may interact. The spatial-context functions make these choices
explicit and return ordinary data frames that can be inspected or reused.

## Configure an example grid

The examples use a coarse grid so that they render quickly.

```{r config}
config <- priogrid::pg_config(
  nrow = 18,
  ncol = 36,
  start_date = as.Date("2020-12-31"),
  end_date = as.Date("2021-12-31"),
  temporal_resolution = "1 year",
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

## Define neighborhoods

`pg_neighbor_table()` creates directed source-neighbor pairs. Queen neighbors
share an edge or corner, whereas rook neighbors must share an edge.

```{r contiguity}
queen <- pg_neighbor_table(20:22, method = "queen", config = config)
rook <- pg_neighbor_table(20:22, method = "rook", config = config)

queen
rook
```

Candidate cells can be restricted explicitly. This is useful when an analysis
contains only a regional or otherwise selected subset of the global grid.

```{r candidates}
pg_neighbor_table(
  pgid = 20:22,
  candidates = 18:25,
  method = "rook",
  config = config
)
```

Distance-band and k-nearest-neighbor definitions include distances between
cell centres in kilometres.

```{r distance-neighbors}
distance_neighbors <- pg_neighbor_table(
  20:22,
  candidates = 18:25,
  method = "distance",
  distance = 1200,
  config = config
)

nearest_neighbors <- pg_neighbor_table(
  20:22,
  candidates = 18:25,
  method = "knn",
  k = 2,
  config = config
)

distance_neighbors
nearest_neighbors
```

## Construct weights

Binary weights treat all listed neighbors equally. Row standardization, which
is enabled by default, makes the weights for each focal cell sum to one.

```{r weights}
rook_weights <- pg_weights(rook)
rook_weights
```

Inverse-distance weights require a table containing `distance_km`.

```{r inverse-distance}
pg_weights(nearest_neighbors, type = "inverse_distance")
```

## Calculate spatial lags

`pg_spatial_lag()` adds a weighted neighboring-cell value to a data frame. If
no weights are supplied, it uses a row-standardized queen neighborhood. Time
columns isolate periods, preventing values from one year from leaking into
another.

```{r spatial-lag}
panel <- data.frame(
  pgid = rep(20:25, 2),
  year = rep(2020:2021, each = 6),
  events = c(0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 1, 1, 2, 4, 0, 2, 3)
)

lagged <- pg_spatial_lag(
  panel,
  value = "events",
  time = "year",
  config = config
)

lagged
```

## Distances and nearest cells

`pg_distance()` supports paired comparisons and all source-destination
combinations. `pg_nearest()` returns an ordered, deterministic nearest-cell
table.

```{r distances}
pg_distance(20:22, 23:25, config = config)
pg_distance(20:21, 22:25, pairwise = FALSE, config = config)

pg_nearest(
  from = 20:22,
  candidates = 18:25,
  n = 2,
  config = config
)
```

## Summarize values within buffers

`pg_buffer_summary()` calculates a sum, mean, count, minimum, or maximum over
cells within a radius. The focal cell is included by default, and time columns
again keep periods separate.

```{r buffers}
buffered <- pg_buffer_summary(
  panel,
  value = "events",
  radius = 1200,
  statistic = "sum",
  time = "year",
  config = config
)

buffered
```

Distances are based on cell centres. A distance-band or buffer therefore does
not mean that the corresponding cell polygons overlap the specified radius.
This distinction should be reported when it is substantively important.
